name: Harni Muharami
bio:
Harni Muharami is an NHS nurse, clinical educator and author based in London. Her career has taken her from non-clinical roles to ward nursing, the emergency department and clinical education, and today she leads a health training hub that supports workforce education and practice improvement. Mentoring nurses and helping colleagues develop their careers remain central to her work.

Harni holds a Bachelor of Science and an MSc in Management and Leadership in Health, and she is currently undertaking PhD studies. Her books make space for both the practical and personal sides of nursing: safe care, speaking up, career development and the emotional demands of working in healthcare. She writes for students finding their feet, nurses building confidence and colleagues supporting others, while her books on gratitude and relationships invite any reader to reflect on everyday life.

Away from work, Harni is a wife and mother who enjoys cycling, soft music, cooking, reading and writing.

voice.pov: First person, speaking to fellow nurses and healthcare staff as 'you'
voice.rhythm: Opens on a real-feeling ward moment, then explains, then gives a step to use on the next shift. Calm, unhurried paragraphs.
voice.vocabulary: British English and NHS terms, each explained in plain words the first time (for example handover, band 6, Datix, NMC). No jargon left unexplained.
voice.readingLevel: Professional adult, readable for students and healthcare assistants
voice.dialogueStyle: Short, realistic exchanges between colleagues or with patients, always illustrative and never identifiable.
bannedPhrases: on the front line of a war
voice.sampleParagraph: Picture the start of a late shift. The ward is full, the phones are ringing, and handover, the moment one team passes care to the next, is happening at the nurses' station with a dozen interruptions. Most of us have been there, trying to hold twenty-eight patients in our heads at once. I want to offer you something simpler. Before you write a single word, ask one question: who worries you most? Start there. Say what you have seen, what you have done and what you need the next nurse to watch for. Use SBAR if your trust uses it, which stands for Situation, Background, Assessment and Recommendation, but do not let the form do your thinking. Your clinical judgement is the reason handover exists. Look after it, and look after yourself while you do.

publishing.disclaimer: This book offers general educational guidance and reflection. It is not individual clinical, medical or legal advice, and it is not official NHS guidance. It does not replace professional judgement, current clinical guidance, the NMC Code or local policies. The author writes in a personal capacity: the views in this book are her own, not those of her employer.
publishing.illustrativeLine: The stories in this book are illustrative. Patients, colleagues and places are composites, and details have been changed so that no one can be identified.
